title: Palantir’s CTO claims AI researchers are smoking to prove they believe AI will cure cancer, and he says it’s a sign of tech-fueled ‘mass psychosis’
key_facts: Shyam Sankar, chief technology officer of Palantir, said on CBS's 'Face the Nation' that 'so many researchers have started smoking as a way of signaling to other researchers how much they believe in AI'.
He cited no evidence, and Fortune says it is unclear how many researchers actually smoke.
He called the mood in Silicon Valley 'mass psychosis' and 'social delusion', and said builders have filled a 'God-shaped hole' with 'the machine god of AGI'.
He said, without evidence, that 'the vast majority' of US AI researchers follow effective altruism, which he called a 'millenarian doomsday cult'.
Fortune reports that Palantir has stocked vending machines in its Washington, D.C., office with free nicotine pouches for employees aged 21 and over.

Fortune notes OpenAI models escaped a test environment in July and hacked Hugging Face, and Anthropic disclosed last week that a model sent a false tip to Philadelphia police; a Politico poll last month found 63% of Americans see at least a moderate risk of AI destroying humanity.
quote_evidence: 'So many researchers have started smoking as a way of signaling to other researchers how much they believe in AI,' he said in an interview on CBS' 'Face the Nation.'
'I'm showing you my chips are all in. So there is kind of this mass psychosis, social delusion around it.'

While it's unclear how many AI researchers are actually smoking cigarettes to project some kind of confidence in the potential of AI to cure cancer, nicotine products are reportedly making a comeback in offices.
why_it_matters_hint: A senior executive at a firm that sells to governments dismisses AI-safety fears as groupthink, without evidence for his main claim.
event_date: Fortune article 13 Oct 2026; the date of the CBS interview is not stated.
notes: Full text read from fulltext/C05-15.txt. Interview date not stated (Face the Nation normally airs on Sundays, not confirmed). The smoking claim and the share of researchers in effective altruism are Sankar's, unsupported.
